newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerian troops at Sierra Leone airport after coup.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian troops at Sierra Leone airport after coup.

text.p: Nigerian troops reinforced Sierra Leone's international airport and leaders of a weekend coup in the West African country on Tuesday expressed concern about talk of a Nigerian counter-attack.
Hundreds of people crammed into beachside hotels for safety as soldiers looted homes and offices and careered round the city in stolen cars.

Police reported protests against the coup in the southern second city of Bo, where the Kamajor civilian militia loyal to President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was ignoring an order to disband, and clashes between troops and Kamajors in the eastern garrison town of Daru.
The new army rulers said they had reopened the land borders and air and sea ports. A dusk to dawn curfew remained in force.

Aid workers and diplomats said Nigerian troops arrived on Monday night to reinforce Nigerians and Ghanaians of the ECOMOG regional intervention force stationed at the airport to defend it from rebel attacks. The airport lies across the river estuary from Freetown and is not easily accessible from the city.
It was not immediately clear whether the Nigerians formed part of reinforcements reported heading for Sierra Leone from neighbouring Liberia on Monday.

"The AFRC is concerned over rumours that our brothers, the Nigerian force, are about to launch an attack," said a statement from the chairman of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Major Johnny Paul Koromah.

"The AFRC is hereby informing the general public to know that it is a baseless rumour. The situation is under control, and all and sundry are hereby requested to go about their normal duties," said the statement, broadcast on national radio.

United Nations staff said a ship had arrived to evacuate U.N. personnel if necessary. The U.N. refugee agency said it would bring most of its staff out. The AFRC promised to cooperate with any evacuation effort for foreign nationals.

Staff at Freetown's Connaught hospital said at least 40 people had been killed in Sunday's fighting, including two Nigerians and several Sierra Leonean soldiers, but ECOMOG Field Commander General Victor Malu said in Lagos on Monday there had been no Nigerian casualties.
The hospital had treated more than 80 wounded.

Shops, banks, schools and markets remained closed on Tuesday despite the coup leaders' appeals to people to return to work. Only a few roadside traders ventured out. The coup leaders ordered civil servants to report for work immediately.

Sources among the political parties that formed the opposition to Kabbah's government said they had been approached to join the government but had declined. They predicted the coup leaders would have trouble forming a credible government.

Troops were searching for ministers of the ousted government, five of whom were reported detained at the military headquarters. Several senior army officers of the rank of lieutenant colonel and above were under house arrest.
The United States called for restoration of the civilian government, joining the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and South Africa in condemning the coup.
Former colonial power Britain on Tuesday deplored the coup and the level of accompanying violence.
The U.N. World Food programme said looters had taken 1,650 tonnes of food aid, 15 vehicles and other equipment from its Freetown warehouses.
Prominent businessman and diamond dealer Jamil Sahid Mohamed said his son Hassan had been shot dead by unidentified men in military uniforms who broke into his house.
Koromah was among those freed when soldiers broke into Freetown's Pademba Road jail early on Sunday. He was accused of planning a coup against Kabbah last September.

Kabbah told the BBC he was still the legitimate president. "I am sad and angry because I am a Sierra Leonean and I see and I hear and I know that a group of hooligans are destroying my country," he said.
